description: Team of young researchers from POLLUB - Lublin University of Technology
summary:
Earth Evidence Atlas helps people investigate a changing planet and test whether the evidence holds. Built by PollubAI for students, educators, and curious citizens, it connects an interactive globe with NASA data, regional time series, statistical analysis, and clear explanations. 

Users choose a variable, place, period, and season; measure change per decade; inspect uncertainty; and test sensitivity to different time windows. Quality-screened MODIS observations, MERRA-2 through NASA POWER, GISTEMP, and GPCP support investigations and comparisons between records. A guided Amazon case introduces the workflow, while the False Alarms lab demonstrates how persistent noise and unusual observations can produce misleading trends. 

The Environmental Resilience Brief brings temperature, rainfall, and soil-wetness indicators together for a selected area. Shareable links, downloadable evidence, and English, Polish, and Spanish interfaces make findings easier to explore and discuss. Our aim is environmental data literacy: understanding not only what appears to be changing, but how confidently the data support that conclusion.
details:
Earth Evidence Atlas is an interactive web application developed by PollubAI for “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”. It connects NASA Earth data with a practical investigation: choose what to measure, select a place, examine change through time, and evaluate its magnitude and statistical significance. The application helps students, educators, and scientifically curious users move from an interesting map to a conclusion they can inspect, question, and share.

Users investigate vegetation greenness, daytime and afternoon land surface temperature, air temperature, precipitation, root-zone soil wetness, and surface temperature anomalies. Prepared regional examples cover Central Europe, north-west India, and the southern Amazon, while global products support wider exploration. Users can draw a rectangular area on the globe; the application reuses available data or retrieves and processes regional NASA data within product-specific limits, with visible progress.

The Globe view combines historical NASA imagery, mapped trends, and animated annual anomalies. Users can select individual grid cells, save places, and open a selected area in Detective. Where a global grid is available, “Find similar areas” locates other areas with comparable average mapped trend rates for the same period and season. This supports geographical exploration without implying that similar rates have the same physical cause.

Detective connects a map, a monthly time series, a seasonal cycle, and a plain-language answer. Results include change per decade, a 95% confidence interval, statistical significance, data coverage, and source limitations. An interactive time-window matrix lets users change the start and end years and distinguish stability of direction from stability of significance. Overlapping windows are identified as related views of the same record, rather than independent confirmations.

The statistical pipeline removes recurring seasonal cycles and accounts for temporal dependence at both monthly and annual scales. A trend must pass both scale-specific checks to be classified as statistically significant. Dependence-adjusted Mann–Kendall tests and Sen’s slope provide additional perspectives, while Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction addresses multiple testing across map cells. Monte Carlo calibration tests cover persistent noise, seasonal selections, missing observations, and changing variance. Remaining difficulty in separating slow natural variability from a trend is documented.

NASA data are essential to the calculations. MODIS Terra and Aqua supply vegetation and land surface temperature observations. Product-specific pixel-quality screening removes rejected observations at native resolution before aggregation. NASA POWER supplies MERRA-2-based air temperature, precipitation, and root-zone soil wetness; NASA GISS GISTEMP supplies surface temperature anomalies. GPCP v2.3 adds a satellite–gauge precipitation record, while NASA GIBS imagery provides geographic context.

Where comparison data are available, the application checks results against another record for the same area, season, and common period. These comparisons include MERRA-2 precipitation versus GPCP, air temperature versus GISTEMP, and Terra versus Aqua surface temperature. They show differences in direction, magnitude, and significance, including disagreements. GPCP’s partial dependence on information also used by MERRA-2 is disclosed. A Validation section brings together dataset comparisons, MODIS quality-screening information, and statistical calibration evidence.

Our central creative contribution is connecting environmental exploration with statistical learning. A step-by-step guided Amazon investigation introduces area selection, trend estimation, uncertainty, season changes, and interpretation. Its results come from the application’s analyses. The False Alarms laboratory uses clearly labelled synthetic data to compare naive and corrected tests, run repeated simulations, and demonstrate how two injected spikes can tilt a fitted trend. These exercises explain why a convincing-looking pattern still needs testing.

The Environmental Resilience Brief extends the investigation into a printable, shareable report. It places air temperature, land surface temperature, precipitation, and soil-wetness trends side by side for a common area, period, and season. Each indicator retains its sources, uncertainty, comparison results, and a link to the full Detective analysis; unavailable data are marked explicitly. The brief can help municipalities, hospitals, and civil or defence infrastructure teams prioritise further local cooling or water-supply assessments. It provides historical regional context, rather than forecasts or facility-level risk ratings.

CSV and JSON exports preserve results, methods, provenance, and limitations, while shareable links reopen selections. The public prototype requires no account and supports English, Polish, and Spanish, with language changes applied without reloading the page. Responsive layouts, light and dark themes, and the guided introduction support different devices and levels of experience.

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, and Rasterio. The frontend uses JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS, Leaflet, and Plotly. Reusable data cubes reduce repeated downloads, and automated tests cover statistical calculations, quality-screening rules, and application behaviour.

The intended impact is stronger environmental data literacy and more transparent interpretation of regional change. This remains an exploratory prototype: spatial resolution, record length, satellite sampling, and reanalysis assumptions constrain its conclusions. Statistical significance does not establish a physical cause, and an interval containing zero does not prove that no change occurred.
dataRefs: MODIS/Terra MOD13A1 V061 – vegetation greenness, NDVI
MODIS/Terra MOD11A2 V061 – daytime land surface temperature
MODIS/Aqua MYD11A2 V061 – afternoon land surface temperature
NASA POWER – monthly T2M, PRECTOTCORR and GWETROOT
NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 – surface temperature anomalies; accessed 2026-11-15
Lenssen et al. (2024) – GISTEMP v4 methodology and observational uncertainty
NASA GIBS – Blue Marble and historical Earth imagery for visual context
projectRefs: Microsoft Planetary Computer – access to NASA MODIS cloud-optimised data
world-atlas – distribution of geographical boundary files
Yale Bright Star Catalogue via d3-celestial – star background
Santer et al. (2000) – trend uncertainty and temporal dependence
Hirsch, Slack and Smith (1982) – seasonal trend analysis
Wilks (2016) – false discovery rate and interpretation of trend maps
Reichle et al. (2017) – MERRA-2 precipitation evaluation and limitations
